subject: Xi got two more months. Canada is still waiting.
bodyMarkdown:
Xi Jinping landed in Washington yesterday and left the tarmac with two more months of tariff peace. Canada has not been in a room with this White House since August, and if your work touches steel, autos, lumber or grain, that gap is the story of your autumn.

## Two more months, and not much else

CNBC reported yesterday that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the United States and China will extend the **Busan agreement**, the truce the two countries struck last October to roll tariffs back and hold off new restrictions, from its November 10 expiry through January 10. Trump met Xi's plane at Joint Base Andrews himself, the first time in eleven years a US president has greeted a foreign leader there. Under the red carpet, the actual complaints have not moved. American officials say Chinese rare earth shipments have not been up to par, and that Beijing is meeting its 25 million tonne soybean commitment while lagging on a separate $17 billion pledge to buy other agricultural goods. I would not call a two month extension progress. A deadline got pushed, which is a different thing, and the new one lands ten days into January.

## An alarm for AI, with no sprinklers

Here is the part I did not expect. Forbes reported on Monday that Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, after eight hours of talks at JPMorgan's Manhattan headquarters, agreed to work toward a notification mechanism: each government tells the other when one of its AI systems causes an incident serious enough to reach national security. Reporters have compared it to the hotline Washington and Moscow built after the Cuban Missile Crisis. Useful, and nobody should mistake it for a limit on what either side builds. CNBC reported on Wednesday that American chip export curbs are not on the table at this summit, and Roll Call reported on Wednesday that Senate Democrats spent the visit pressing for floor votes on export control bills stuck behind the defence authorization bill, with Chuck Schumer saying Trump "could take action today."

## Canada is the country without a chair

Ours is the awkward seat. Talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down on the night of August 21, and Mark Carney said the next day that the American terms were "uneconomic" and "unfair." US tariffs of 50 per cent on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods went ahead under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, and Canada matched from September 8 with 50 per cent duties on American steel, furniture, dairy, appliances, clothing and electronics. CNBC reported on September 3 that Carney will resume talks "when the Americans are ready." Meanwhile the Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2 and flagged new tariffs and high energy prices as upside risk to inflation. Statistics Canada put August inflation at 3.0 per cent on September 14, the same as July.

## The takeaway

Watch January 10 the way you watch a chess clock, because that is the date the two largest economies have to produce something real or reset again. For Canada the date that matters is whenever Washington picks up the phone, and nothing this week suggests it is soon. If you are pricing a renovation or any input that crosses the border, plan on 50 per cent duties holding through the autumn rather than betting on a thaw. The Bank of Canada meets again in October, and with inflation parked at 3.0 per cent I do not expect a cut to rescue anyone.
